description: Soy científico de datos y programador, cuento con habilidades para la creación de entornos lúdicos de aprendizaje. Busco formar un equipo diverso, sobre todo centrado en el apartado artístico y creativo.
summary:
Mission Mars: Survival Base! is a bilingual (English/Spanish) web game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player commands a Mars base for 10 sols and must share a 100 kW generator among three modules that need 150 kW: Life Support (40 kW), Farm (50 kW) and Radiation Shields (60 kW). Every choice has a cost: turning on the shields during a solar storm means turning off the farm, and food goes down; leaving them off keeps the harvest but radiation lowers crew health. Consequences build up from sol to sol.

Solar storms are based on real NASA DONKI data: each sol is one real day from May 14 to 23, 2024, and a storm happens when at least one coronal mass ejection has an estimated arrival at Mars that day. After every sol, a Sol Report explains what happened and why, and a Final Mission Report summarizes the player's decisions and the key lesson: on Mars we can't have it all, and every resource counts.
details:
What it does: Mission Mars: Survival Base! is a turn-based web game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player manages a Mars base for 10 sols. A 100 kW generator cannot power all three modules at once (150 kW in total), so the player must choose what to keep on. Each sol, the game applies the consequences: without Life Support, health drops; without the Farm, food drops; during a solar storm without Shields, radiation lowers health. Moving on with more than 100 kW causes a blackout. The player wins by reaching the end of Sol 10 with health and food above 0 %.

How it uses NASA data: each sol is a real day from May 14 to 23, 2024. We downloaded the coronal mass ejections (CMEs) recorded in NASA DONKI for that period and marked a storm on the days when at least one CME had an estimated arrival at Mars (WSA-ENLIL model). The alert shows the real date and number of CMEs. Arrivals are model estimates, not measurements on Mars, and the energy, health and food values are simplified game values; the game says so in the Credits panel.

Benefits and impact: kids learn by doing that engineering on Mars means trade-offs: protecting the crew can cost food, and saving food can cost health. A Sol Report explains every consequence in simple words, and a Final Mission Report shows the player's real decisions and a strategy tip. The game is bilingual (English/Spanish), works on computers, netbooks and tablets, and info buttons open by tap. After testing it with a child, we shortened the start screen and added a 3-step "How to play" guide.

Tools: React 18, Vite 5, lucide-react icons, GitHub and Vercel. No database and no live API: the DONKI data is stored in the project, so no API key is exposed.

Team: Franco Lescano (original prototype, game rules, interface sketch and module illustrations), Soledad Rumiche (educational design, narrative and presentation), Pablo Vallejo (coordination, development and integration, publishing and testing).
